# The impacts of companion AI on human relationships: risks, benefits, and design considerations

- Open Forum
- Open access
- Published: 16 April 2025

- Kim Malfacini 1 

## 1 Introduction

AI applications intended for companionship have increased in both availability and capabilities in recent years, alongside a spike in loneliness (Johnson 2023; Murthy 2023). According to a 2024 analysis by venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, companion AI makes up 16 of the top 100 AI apps based on web traffic and monthly active users (Moore 2024). Moreover, today’s AI applications have a greater command of human language, an increasing capacity for storing memories, and more varied modalities to support an increasing diversity of experiences, a known driver in the development and deepening of emotional relationships (Skjuve et al. 2022).

At the same time, people are increasingly lonely. The US Surgeon General has classified loneliness as an epidemic with severe ramifications for well-being (Murthy 2023) and the World Health Organization has declared the health impacts of loneliness as on par with smoking 15 cigarettes a day (Johnson 2023). The proliferation of companion AI at a time of great collective emotional need begs critical questions. Can AI truly be a companion, whether platonic or romantic? What does engaging with companion AI as one would a person mean for our understanding of relationships? Even if we accept that companion AI can make a person happy, is it good for us? How might it affect our other relationships? What societal implications might its widespread adoption have? While there is an increasing volume of research on the impacts of companion AI relationships on users, there is a dearth of research on the impacts of companion AI on human relationships (Guingrich and Graziano 2023). This paper aims to contribute to the advancement of needed discourse on these questions.

The apprehension regarding companion AI’s impacts on human relationships can be boiled down to two primary concerns. One, that companion AI meets our social and emotional needs to such a degree that it replaces human relationships (herein, the replacement concern). And two, that we become accustomed to not giving as much in relationships because companion AI demands less—or differently—of us (herein, the deskilling concern) (Turkle 2011; Ciriello et al. 2024). Under this theory, as companion AI learns to meet our needs more, we learn to meet each others’ less. The widespread realisation of either of these concerns risks eroding something fundamental to our humanity: not just our competence in or desire to build relationships with other people, but our more fundamental capacities to love and be loved, to belong and to keep. Our social and moral tapestry might feel quite different when it is no longer comprised entirely of human threads.

We are early in the companion AI adoption curve, but judging by the recent uptick in consumer use and continued expansion of capabilities, further increases in adoption seem likely (Moore 2024). It is thus critical that we better understand the impacts companion AI may have on us as individuals and to society more broadly. This paper intends to make two contributions to the literature and discourse on impacts of companion AI: a categorisation of the primary risks and benefits posed by companion AI to human relationships, and an argument for designing companion AI to actively support human relationships.

Section 2 briefly defines companion AI and substantiates the focus of this inquiry on its impact on human relationships. Section 3 explores the risks and benefits companion AI poses to human relationships and highlights potentially vulnerable user demographics. Section 4 argues that we should design it in a manner that supports human relationships through social upskilling and motivation and provides design recommendations to those ends.

## 2 Defining companion AI and situating this inquiry

This inquiry is primarily focused on companion AI, AI products purpose-built to meet users’ emotional and social needs. Herein, we adopt the definition of companionship as “a mutually supportive and emotionally enriching bond formed between two individuals who provide each other with a lasting sense of care” (Ciriello et al. 2024). Companion AI is a subset of conversational AI, AI systems that communicate with users primarily through text or voice using natural language (Ruane, Birhane, and Ventresque 2019). While much conversational AI is designed to mimic human interaction, companion AI is notable for its design to foster the illusion of social presence and relational continuity, making it function as a social agent designed to elicit social and moral responses (Dautenhahn 1998; Leong and Selinger 2019).

Some of the most popular companion AI apps include Nomi, Kindroid, Replika, Candy.ai, and Character.ai, (Roose 2024a). Companion AI are typically customisable; their name, persona, disposition, background, and, in some cases, avatar and voice are set by the user. This customisation provides a feeling of uniqueness and authenticity, which facilitates interaction and paves the way for development of emotional attachments (Pentina et al. 2023). Today’s companion AI have text, image, and voice capabilities, and Replika, among the most popular companion AI services, has an augmented reality feature in which users can project their companion in the room, similar to the companion AI Joi in Blade Runner 2049 (Roose 2024a).

This inquiry is not primarily focused on general purpose chatbots such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude, which are not explicitly designed for companionship. These companies have acknowledged the emotional reliance risk of their AI products (OpenAI 2024b), however, and many individuals nevertheless build intimate relationships with these chatbots (Lee et al. 2021, Roose 2024c). Given companion AI products are marketed as such (Ciriello et al. 2024), they may be more likely to attract users with unfulfilled social or emotional needs, making their risks potentially a greater cause for concern.

This inquiry is focused not on the impacts of companion AI on users, but rather on the impacts of human–AI relationships on peripheral human–human relationships. Such focus is warranted for two reasons. For one, while academic focus on the impacts of companion AI on users has increased in recent years, there is as yet limited research, particularly longitudinal empirical research, on the impacts of companion AI on relationships between and among humans. And secondly, while we can debate the degree to which human–AI relationships may deliver benefits to individuals that otherwise stem from human–human relationships, we should be quite skeptical that human–AI relationships could deliver anywhere near the benefits to society collectively that human–human relationships have and continue to provide. This argument requires a brief exploration of the importance of connection across academic disciplines.

### 2.1 The importance of human connection across disciplines

Significant theory and research exists across academic disciplines on the importance of human relationships to both individual and collective well-being. Philosophers have long heralded the value of companionship. Aristotle urged friendships were critical to accessing “eudaimonia” or human flourishing and devoted two books of his Nicomachean Ethics to the topic (Kraut 2022). Importantly, he argued it is critical not merely to possess but to exercise one’s capacities, as exercise facilitates refinement. In other words, it is insufficient to be able to be a good friend; one must pursue friendships—actually be a good friend—which further refines and builds one’s social capacity.

From a philosophical perspective, human companionship is valuable regardless of the theory of well-being to which one subscribes, whether hedonism, desire satisfaction, or objective list theory. Friendships and romantic relationships are typically pleasurable, satisfying hedonism, and, with perhaps some limited exceptions, they are desired, satisfying desire satisfaction. Many prominent accounts of objective list theory also hold some variation on companionship as a stated good (Nussbaum 2007; Parfit 1986; Finnis 1980).

Psychology similarly places great importance on human relationships. Early twentieth century psychologist Alfred Adler emphasised the importance of social needs to health and well-being, introducing the notion of “social interest”: our capacity for cooperation with and belonging to other individuals (1938). Adler argued social interest is critical for individuals to achieve and maintain a healthy personality and for society to advance humanity in a positive direction.

Later psychologists continued to highlight the importance of companionship to well-being. Self-determination theory, introduced in the 1970s, maintains relatedness, the need to feel connected and belong to others, as one of three fundamental psychological needs, alongside autonomy and competence (Ryan and Deci 2017). According to this theory, only when these needs are satisfied can an individual attain well-being, self-motivate, and grow. This framework has been extensively validated through empirical research (Vansteenkiste et al. 2020).

More recently, Martin Seligman’s positive psychology transformed the field from a primary focus on the identification and treatment of psychological disorders to a focus on identifying and building positive human behaviours and mentalities (Seligman and Csikszentmihalyi 2000). Through positive psychology, Seligman advanced the PERMA framework, which holds that Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, and Accomplishment are required for flourishing. Contemporary psychology research has further confirmed that humans are inclined to create social attachments—and accordingly inclined to resist their dissolution—and that both social belonging and the lack thereof have significant impacts on health and well-being (Baumeister and Leary 1995; Holt-Lunstad et al. 2010). The negative health consequences of social isolation, including increased mortality risk, underscore the importance of human relationships (Holt-Lunstad et al. 2015).

Further, social relationships have benefits for the well-being of society more broadly. Sociologists emphasise the importance of relationships to both individual and collective well-being. Émile Durkheim established social cohesion, which he defined as interdependence between individuals, as a necessity for the health and functioning of any society (Fonseca et al. 2018). Anthropologists have further identified social collaboration and cohesion as pivotal factors in human survival and evolution (Boyd and Richerson 2009). Human relationships have facilitated the development and sharing of practices that have enabled societies to collectively solve problems and adapt to changing environments (Osher et al. 2018). Collectively, this scholarship puts forth a compelling case that social relationships are fundamental not only to individual well-being but as the foundation for societal stability, adaptation, and progress.

### 2.2 The value of human relationships versus companion AI relationships

Given social relationships are critical, does it necessarily follow that human–human relationships should be privileged over human–AI relationships? It seems possible that some subset of the benefits individuals derive from companionship might be generated through human–AI relationships. Might companion AI provide an individual with a sense of social belonging that begets positive health impacts? Might companion AI relationships reduce the mortality risk associated with social isolation? These are empirical questions that future research can and must answer.
